sense: the grated peel of a lemon or orange

terms.grammar: cortex, corticis m., with the perfect participle of rādō
terms.comment: A description of ours. We have found no Latin word for zest in Lewis & Short, Traupman, Morgan–Owens (which lists the English headword with no Latin), or Levi–Bini. Cortex is the peel (see “peel”), rādere the verb for grating (see “grate”); only the coloured skin is wanted, summus cortex. Lewis & Short glosses Vitruvius’s scobis citrea (8.3.8) as grated lemon peel, but there an oil smells like it, and it more likely means the sawdust of the fragrant citrus wood; it is not used here.

terms.gloss: shavings of peel: zest in strips
evidence: Plin. NH 15.67: rāmentīs abietis (Lewis & Short s.v. rāmenta)
terms.comment: Rāmenta, from rādō, are classically shavings and scrapings, larger than scobis (Lewis & Short): for zest taken off in strips. A description of ours.

phrases.latin: Summum tantum corticem rāde; quod subest album, amārum est.
phrases.english: Grate only the outer peel; the white underneath is bitter.
Add the zest to the dough.

phrases.latin: anēsum, cumīnum, adipis P. II, cāseī lībram, et dē virgā laurī dērāditō, eōdem additō
phrases.english: aniseed, cumin, two pounds of fat, a pound of cheese, and scrape some off a bay twig, and add it all to the same bowl

sources: Lewis & Short: cortex · Lewis & Short: rado · Lewis & Short: ramenta
